title: Two Weeks Notice
full_review:
Sandra Bullock and Hugh Grant's talents for light comedy are all for naught in the bland romantic comedy, "Two Weeks Notice" (Warner Bros.).

For fans of the two, the opening credits featuring actual photos of each from babyhood to adolescence may prove more appealing than the movie itself.

The paper-thin story has real estate magnate George Wade (Grant) getting activist lawyer Lucy Kelson (Bullock) to work for him on the condition he not tear down her Coney Island neighborhood's community center.

Soon he is dependent on her to make every itty-bitty decision for him while she becomes frustrated with such trivial concerns. Informing him she's out the door in two weeks, she's also put off when he instantly hires as her replacement a red-headed hottie, June (Alicia Witt), with gold-digger moves.

Lucy's jealous, George is dumb and June is obvious, a combination which doesn't make for a smart comedy with romantic sparkle.

Writer-director Marc Lawrence's flat script is the chief offender. With such banal dialogue as "you have to use your powers for good rather than evil," the cliches are all in place. Bullock is game to repeat her winsome comic klutziness and Grant is back to twittering his eyelashes for laughs, but the situations and the banter between them is ordinary, not screwball or clever. At least, Donald Trump's cameo as a fellow land developer adds unintended comedy with his wildly outdated hairstyle.

Much time is given to establishing that Lucy has been an idealistic protestor since birth; her parents raised her to be a committed lawyer and social activist. (You also know this by the drab flower-child outfits she wears until she has to wear monotonous power suits in the corporate world.)

But we have no idea why George is such a self-absorbed airhead (or why Lucy is unconsciously in love with him since his chief asset, money, means nothing to her). One glance at June and we know everything we need to know about her and what she's after. So the romantic triangle crawls along to its assured outcome without delivering much entertainment.

Because of sexual situations and references and fleeting drunkenness, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
